extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of humorous essays/sketches (aspiring humorists, general literary readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and illustrative examples for producing short humorous sketches and topical satire, especially dialogue-driven character pieces and pantomime-style material. Emphasises tone, character voice, and techniques for turning ordinary or political subjects into comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innocent raillery, free from partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The proper attitude to have assumed towards it was that of innocent raillery, free from all trace of partisanship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating political or topical subjects (e.g., a pantomime referencing the 'Fiscal question'), aim for a light, non-partisan mockery that offends neither side; be topical without taking a political stance. Context: Johnson (editor) wants a 'bright, amusing resumé of the whole problem that should give offence to neither side.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer light, playfully witty remarks over boisterous humour for some audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Pilson... does not need anything boisterously funny. A few playfully witty remarks on the subject will be the ideal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the scale and temperament of the audience or venue: some audiences respond best to gentle, witty touches rather than loud or broad comedy. Tone selection matters (subtle wit vs. boisterous farce).

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the amusing side of anything (including misfortune)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Everything has its amusing side... Hardly a misfortune that can happen to mankind but has produced its comic literature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for comic potential across subjects — disasters, wars, funerals, weddings, natural catastrophes — and reframe them as material for humorous stories (examples given: earthquake, cyclone, flood, thunderstorm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use literal misunderstandings / naive interpretations for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedic exchanges where a character takes metaphors or figures of speech literally (e.g., explaining 'dumping' as physically throwing goods onto shores).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let a character's earnest literalness expose absurdities in common expressions or political/economic language; the resulting misunderstandings create humour through contrast between speaker's jargon and lay comprehension (demonstrated in the Mrs. Wilkins 'dumping' dialogue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ vivid character voice and colloquial/dialect speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour driven by strongly-drawn, colloquial characters (e.g., Mrs. Wilkins' working-class speech and idioms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distinctive syntax, pronunciation, and pragmatic worldviews to create empathy and comic contrast with the narrator or other characters; dialect can both entertain and advance social commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration and absurdity to satirise arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hyperbole and reductio ad absurdum (e.g., 'It will cost nobody anything, and will result in everybody being better off.'; mine-owner as an archangel; 'meat extract, prepared exclusively from new-born infants').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push premises to grotesque or absurd conclusions to lampoon economic or moral reasoning; extreme images and unlikely analogies emphasise the satirical point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast paired situations to reveal absurdities
rubrics_metrics.description: Set two comparable but different contexts side by side (e.g., hotel service vs private domestic service) to highlight ironies and generate sympathy/laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parallel descriptions to show how small differences in arrangement (hours, autonomy, expectations) change human experience, producing both comedic and critical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose unrealistic social expectations via hyperbole
rubrics_metrics.description: Present employers' or society's standards as impossibly high (e.g., the 'right gal' whose 'place is up in 'eaven with a 'arp').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirise class expectations by exaggerating the traits demanded of servants or dependents; contrast stated ideals with practical realities to evoke humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate escalating hypothetical alternatives for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedic internal deliberation listing increasingly absurd or violent options (e.g., considering 'knocking the fellow down and making a bolt'), used to dramatise frustration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure thought processes as a sequence of possible responses that escalate from reasonable to absurd; the escalation itself functions as the comic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirise the authority of statistics and official returns
rubrics_metrics.description: 'You would be surprised, Mrs. Wilkins, how many things can be proved from Board of Trade Returns!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lampoon bureaucratic or statistical certainty by claiming contradictory conclusions can be 'proved' from the same data; use this to undermine pretensions of expertise or to mock public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use topical review format to incorporate current events gently
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual pantomime as 'a review of the year's doings' — topical references expected but to be handled with innocence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing seasonal or periodic entertainments that summarise current events, include topical touches to be 'up-to-date' while keeping tone light and non-partisan so as to entertain a broad audience (editorial desire to 'steer clear of politics, but... be up-to-date').

rubrics_metrics.name: Role-reversal and practical suggestions as comedic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose role changes or pragmatic remedies (e.g., mistress taking her turn in domestic chores) to expose contradictions in social rhetoric about 'dignity of labour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use suggested social experiments or reversals of expectation to both critique and amuse — presenting a plausible-sounding but pointedly comic 'solution' to a social problem highlights hypocrisy or complacency.
